findings.title: p-values in scientific notation are read as 'p = 1', producing HIGH-severity recompute errors and 'impossible p-value' notes
findings.detail: The `|1(?:\.0+)?|` branch of the PV alternation comes before the exponent branch and nothing anchors the end of the match. So for 'p = 1.5 × 10-5', 'p = 1e-5' or 'p = 1.2E-6' the regex captures just '1'. recompute() then reports p = 1 against a computed p of about 1.6e-5, flags `decision=True`, and check() raises a HIGH `stats.recompute` (an integrity finding, confidence 0.85). IMPOSSIBLE_RE at line 176 makes a related mistake: `[1-9]\d*\.\d*[1-9]\d*` matches the mantissa '1.5' of '1.5 × 10-5', and `[2-9]\b` matches the '2' of 'p = 2.3e-5', so ordinary genomics-style p-values are reported as 'never above 1'. I reproduced this with the venv: recompute('t(28) = 5.20, p = 1.5 × 10-5') returns reported 'p = 1' with decision True. impossible('P = 2.3e-5') and impossible('p = 3.1 × 10-4') both return hits.
findings.failure_scenario: A biology paper writes 't(28) = 5.20, P = 1.5 × 10−5' (the PDF text becomes '10-5' after the minus is replaced). The report shows a HIGH integrity signal: 'p-value cannot follow from the statistic; changes the conclusion at p = 0.05'. On its own this adds about 18 points to the risk score.
findings.fix: Parse the full p-value token before deciding anything. Put the exponent forms first and add a terminator, for example PV = r"[pP]\s*([<>=≤≥]|<|>)\s*((?:\d(?:\.\d+)?\s*(?:[eE]|[×x]\s*10\^?\s*)-?\s*\d+)|0?\.\d+|1(?:\.0+)?)(?![\d.])", then convert the '×10-5' form to float. In IMPOSSIBLE_RE add a negative lookahead `(?!\s*(?:[eE]|[×x]\s*10))` after the value, and require `(?![\d.eE])`.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real. I reproduced it with the project venv.

**The p-value regex (stats.py:22)**
- The PV alternation `(0?\.\d+|1(?:\.0+)?|\d(?:\.\d+)?[eE]-?\d+)` has nothing after it that marks the end of the number. Python's regex takes the first branch that matches, so `1(?:\.0+)?` captures just "1" from any p-value whose mantissa begins with 1:
  - 'p = 1.5 × 10-5'
  - 'p = 1.5e-5'
  - 'p = 1e-5'
  - 'P = 1.5 x 10-5'
- Because of this, the `[eE]` branch can never be reached for these mantissas.
- The `×10-5` notation is not supported by any branch.
- check() at line 198 replaces U+2212 with '-' before matching, so the PDF form '10−5' becomes '10-5' and hits this bug.

**Effect in recompute (lines 86-110)**
- recompute('t(28) = 5.20, p = 1.5 × 10-5') returns reported 'p = 1', computed about 1.6e-5, decision=True. The other three strings above give the same result.
- check() (lines 200-211) then raises a HIGH `stats.recompute` finding with confidence 0.85, saying the conclusion changes at p = 0.05.
- Mantissas 2-9 written as `×10` avoid the false finding, but only by accident. For example, 'p = 2.3 × 10-5' matches nothing, so the test is silently skipped.

**IMPOSSIBLE_RE (line 176)**
It does misfire:
- impossible('P = 2.3e-5') returns 'P = 2'.
- impossible('p = 3.1 × 10-4'), 'p = 1.5 × 10-5' and 'p = 2.3 × 10^-5' return '3.1', '1.5' and '2.3'.

That finding is only "low" severity with confidence 0.6 (line 240). It is a false positive, but less serious than the HIGH recompute finding.

**Is it realistic?**
Yes. Writing p-values as 'P = 1.5 × 10−5' is routine in genomics and biology papers, so this happens with ordinary input.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Change PV so it captures the full scientific-notation token, with the exponent forms tried first and a terminator at the end:

PV = r"[pP]\s*([<>=≤≥]|<|>)\s*(\d(?:\.\d+)?\s*(?:[eE]\s*|[×xX*·]\s*10\s*\^?\s*)[-−]?\s*\d+|0?\.\d+|1(?:\.0+)?)(?![\d.])"

Then in recompute(), turn rep_s into a float through a helper before the existing float(rep_s) call, e.g. `m2 = re.match(r"(\d(?:\.\d+)?)\s*(?:[eE]|[×xX*·]\s*10\s*\^?)\s*([-−]?)\s*(\d+)$", rep_s); rep = float(m2[1]) * 10 ** (-(int(m2[3])) if m2[2] else int(m2[3]))`. Also make _consistent treat the '×10' form like the 'e' form; right now it only checks for 'e' in rep_s.lower(), so this should be a has-exponent flag. For a bare '10-5' the minus sign comes from the U+2212 replacement, so keep treating '-' as negative.

In IMPOSSIBLE_RE, stop it from matching a mantissa, for example:

IMPOSSIBLE_RE = re.compile(r"\b[pP]\s*=\s*(0?\.0+|[1-9]\d*\.\d*[1-9]\d*|[2-9])(?![\d.])(?!\s*(?:[eE]\s*[-−+]?\d|[×xX*·]\s*10))(?![.\d]*%)")

The original `\b` after the group was what let 'P = 2' match inside '2.3e-5'. In the replacement, `(?![\d.])` stops the value from ending partway through a number, and the exponent lookahead rejects any mantissa that is followed by e-notation or ×10.

findings.title: duplicate_block compares a column with itself shifted by one period, so every periodic or long-format column becomes a HIGH integrity hit
findings.detail: The only guard for self-matches is `if ca == cb and abs(sa - sb) < WINDOW: continue`. A column that repeats a non-arithmetic pattern with period ≥ 6, such as time points 0,5,15,30,60,120 per subject, a log dose series 0.1,0.3,1,3,10,30, or ELISA standard-curve concentrations 1000,500,250,125,62.5,31.25, matches itself at offset 6. The extension loop (lines 146-151) then grows the match to almost the whole column. `_trivial` only rejects constant step sizes. I reproduced this: a long-format table of 20 subjects × 6 time points gave `data.duplicate_block` 'Identical run of 114 values in two places', severity high, kind integrity, risk_score 25, from honest data.
findings.failure_scenario: Any Source Data file in long format (subject, time, value), and any plate-reader export with repeated standard curves, produces a HIGH 'copied block' integrity signal and pushes the verdict to 'Worth a closer look'.
findings.fix: Drop self-comparisons (ca == cb) unless the values are precise (mean sig digits ≥ 3) and the column has high cardinality. In addition, skip columns whose distinct-value ratio is low (for example len(set(raw)) < 0.5*len(raw)), and extend `_trivial` to reject geometric progressions and windows whose values all occur many times in the column.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real, and I reproduced it. In engine/paperinspector/datacheck.py, _duplicate_blocks (lines 125-151) indexes every 6-value window of every column. The only self-match guard is line 141, `if ca == cb and abs(sa - sb) < WINDOW: continue`. When a column repeats a pattern every 6 or more rows, the windows at offsets 0 and 6 are identical. Their distance is exactly WINDOW, so the guard does not skip them. The forward extension (lines 149-151) then compares the column against itself shifted by one period and grows the match to len - period values.

_trivial (lines 93-103) does not filter these windows. It only rejects windows with fewer than 4 distinct values, a constant step size, or all small integers. Time points like 0,5,15,30,60,120 have no constant step, and 60 and 120 are not small, so they pass. Halving dilutions like 1000,500,250,125,62.5,31.25 pass for the same reasons.

Severity is set to high when ln >= 10 (line 164). models.py line 133 puts data.duplicate_block in INTEGRITY, so it counts toward the risk score. pipeline.py line 372 calls datacheck.check(src.tables) with no extra filtering.

I ran this in the project .venv. A long-format table of 20 subjects × 6 time points, each with a random 3-decimal value, gave a high integrity finding: 'Identical run of 114 values in two places'. A plate column holding 4 repeats of a 7-point 2-fold dilution series gave a high finding: 'Identical run of 21 values', rows 2-22 vs 9-29 of the same column. Long-format Source Data and repeated standard curves are common, so honest uploads will trigger this.
verdict.corrected_fix: Treat a column matching itself with a periodic shift as structure, not copying. For ca == cb, compute the shift p = |sb - sa|. If a.raw[i] == a.raw[i+p] holds for almost the whole column (the extended run ln >= 0.8*(len - p)), skip it as a design/repeat column. Also skip a self-match outright when the column has low cardinality: len(set(c.raw)) <= 0.5*len(c.raw), or the window's values each appear at least 3 times in the column. Separately, extend _trivial to reject geometric progressions (np.allclose of successive ratios, e.g. dilution series) and windows whose values are all among the column's most frequent values. Keep cross-column and cross-file matches unchanged, so real copied blocks are still caught. Add a regression test with a long-format subject×time table and a repeated dilution-series column; neither should produce data.duplicate_block.

findings.title: Formula-linked cells are reported as copied data (HIGH integrity)
findings.detail: _duplicate_blocks works on data_only values and never consults `Table.formulas`. In honest workbooks one sheet often references another, for example a 'Fig2a' sheet with =Raw!A2 down a column, or a chart-data sheet. Those values are identical by construction. I reproduced this: a Raw sheet plus a Fig2a sheet whose cells are '=Raw!A{i}' gave 'Identical run of 30 values in two places', severity high, integrity, score 32.
findings.failure_scenario: An author's Source Data xlsx has a summary sheet that references the raw sheet. The scan reports a high-severity copy-paste signal.
findings.fix: Before reporting a block, check t.formulas for the cells of either copy (cell_ref(idx[k], j)). If most of them are formulas, in particular references to another sheet or cell, skip the block or downgrade it to an info note ('values linked by formula').

verdict.reason:
The bug is real, and I reproduced it.

How the values reach the check:
- `read_xlsx` in engine/paperinspector/tables.py:82-83 opens the workbook twice. The cell values come from the `data_only=True` copy. That copy holds the cached results, which Excel saves into every workbook.
- Formulas are collected separately into `Table.formulas` (tables.py:100-104).

Where the check goes wrong:
- `_duplicate_blocks` (datacheck.py:125-182) builds its windows only from `Col.raw` (the values). It never looks at `t.formulas`.
- The only place `formulas` affects any decision is `_formulas` (RAND detection, line 227) and `_generator` (line 440). Neither applies here.
- Nothing downstream suppresses the finding. pipeline.py:372 adds the datacheck findings straight to the results, and `data.duplicate_block` is in the INTEGRITY set (models.py:133), so it counts toward the score.

Reproduction: I ran the project venv with two Table objects matching what an Excel-saved workbook produces.
- A 'Raw' sheet held 30 three-decimal values.
- A 'Fig2a' sheet held the same values, with `formulas` set to `{'A2':'=Raw!A2', ...}`.
- `check()` returned `data.duplicate_block`, severity high, confidence 0.8, titled 'Identical run of 30 values in two places'.

This setup is realistic: Source Data sheets that reference a raw sheet are common. The one limit is that workbooks written by openpyxl without cached values would load as None and not trigger it, but files saved by Excel or LibreOffice do have cached values.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `_duplicate_blocks`, after computing the final block (ca, sa, cb, sb, ln) and before adding the Finding, count how many of the block's cells in each copy are formulas: `n = sum(cell_ref(c.idx[k], c.j) in c.t.formulas for k in range(s, s + ln))`, computed for both copies.

If either copy is mostly formulas (for example at least 80% of `ln`):
- If the formulas are plain references (match something like `^=\s*('?[^!]+'?!)?\$?[A-Z]{1,3}\$?\d+\s*$`), skip the block or report it as an info-level `data.linked_block` quality note ('values linked by formula to ...').
- Otherwise downgrade it to a quality note rather than a high-severity integrity finding.

Do this before the `used.add((ca, cb))` dedup, so that skipping a formula-linked pair does not hide a genuine copy between the same two columns.

Add a test: a Raw sheet plus a Fig2a sheet of `=Raw!A{i}` formulas should give no integrity finding, and the same pair without formulas should still give one.

findings.title: PCT_RE has catastrophic backtracking: a scan hangs on long letter runs
findings.detail: In `(?:[a-z]+\s*){0,3}\(`, `\s*` can be empty, so a run of letters can be split into up to 3 pieces in O(n^3) ways, and finditer repeats that for each start position. Measured: '12 of 40 ' + 'a'*500 takes 0.74 s, and 'a'*2000 did not finish in 40 s. stats.check runs on every supplementary paper (pipeline.py 366). DOCX supplements put each paragraph on one line, so a DNA, protein or primer sequence after 'construct 1 of 3' (re.I makes [a-z] match ACGT) creates exactly this input.
findings.failure_scenario: A supplementary .docx contains 'Fragment 1 of 2 ATGCGT…' with a 5 kb unbroken sequence. The analysis thread spins for many minutes or hangs, and the run never finishes.
findings.fix: Make the words unambiguous: `(?:[a-z]{1,25}\s+){0,3}\(` (whitespace required between words), or use a possessive `(?:[a-z]++\s*){0,3}` (Python 3.11+). Alternatively cap the gap with `[^()]{0,40}\(`.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real. I confirmed it in the code and reproduced it.

**Where the pattern is used.** `PCT_RE` is defined at `engine/paperinspector/stats.py:135`. `percent()` (line 140) runs it with `finditer`. `check()` calls `percent()` at line 221, on text that line 198 has already flattened to a single line with `" ".join(paper.text.split())`. So any long run of letters reaches the regex, whatever the source format. `pipeline.py:364` runs `stats.check` on the main paper, and `pipeline.py:366` runs it on every supplementary paper.

**Why it is slow.** In `(?:[a-z]+\s*){0,3}`, the `\s*` can match nothing, so a run of n letters can be split into up to 3 words in O(n^2) ways. Each split is then tried against the failing `\(`. The match only starts after a "k of n" or "k/n" prefix, which is common in papers (for example "Fragment 1 of 2", "construct 1 of 3"). With `re.I`, `[a-z]` also matches upper-case ACGT sequences.

**Measured times** (I timed the regex directly, because scipy is not installed here so the module would not import), on 'Fragment 1 of 2 ' + 'ATGC'*k:

| Letters | Time |
|---|---|
| 200 | 0.05 s |
| 400 | 0.37 s |
| 800 | 2.98 s |
| 1600 | 23.5 s |

That is roughly cubic growth. A 5 kb sequence would take many minutes to hours, so the analysis thread effectively hangs as described.

**The reviewer's first fix needs a change.** Their `[a-z]{1,25}\s+` requires whitespace before the parenthesis. That would stop matching inputs the current regex accepts, such as "12 of 40 mice(30%)". The corrected fix below keeps that behaviour.
verdict.corrected_fix:
At engine/paperinspector/stats.py:135, lock each word so the regex cannot split a run of letters. Use a negative lookahead (works on any Python 3):
PCT_RE = re.compile(r"\b(\d{1,5})\s*(?:/|of|out of)\s*(\d{1,5})\s*(?:[a-z]+(?![a-z])\s*){0,3}\(\s*(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d+)?)\s*%\s*\)", re.I)
On Python 3.11+ you can write the possessive form instead: `(?:[a-z]++\s*){0,3}`.

Verified results:
- 1600 letters: 0.0001 s; 20000 letters: 0.0006 s.
- Still matches '12 of 40 mice(30%)', '3/4 (75 %)' and '5 of 10 treated animals (50%)'.
- Still rejects a 4-word gap.

I advise against the reviewer's `\s+` version, because it drops matches like 'mice(30%)' where no space comes before the parenthesis.

Also add a regression test that runs percent() on 'Fragment 1 of 2 ' + 'ACGT'*1000 and checks it finishes in under 1 s.

findings.title: Quadratic block extension: two identical long columns take minutes
findings.detail: For each indexed window shared by two columns the code extends backwards and forwards (lines 146-151) before checking `seen`. Two identical columns of length L therefore do L extensions of O(L) each, O(L^2) in total. Measured: L=1000 takes 0.17 s, 2000 takes 0.65 s and 4000 takes 2.5 s, so the 20000-row cap means about 60 s per column pair. Omics supplements often repeat a gene-length or control column across sheets or files, and every extra copy multiplies the cost. Memory also grows: the window index holds up to 400 columns × 20000 rows of 6-tuples.
findings.failure_scenario: A Source Data workbook repeats a 20000-row annotation column in 5 sheets. That gives 10 pairs at about 60 s each, so the data-check stage runs for 10 minutes or more.
findings.fix: Only start an extension at the beginning of a block: skip occurrence (sa, sb) when sa > 0, sb > 0 and a.raw[sa-1] == b.raw[sb-1]. Or keep a set of covered (ca, cb, sa - sb) diagonals and skip windows already inside a reported block. Also cap the number of occurrences per key (for example 20).

verdict.reason: I confirmed this from the code and by measuring it. In engine/paperinspector/datacheck.py:125-156, `_duplicate_blocks` indexes every non-trivial 6-value window. For each pair of occurrences that share a key, it walks backwards (lines 146-148) and forwards (lines 150-151) to the full block, and only then checks `seen` (line 153). Two identical numeric columns of length L give L shared keys, one pair each. Every pair re-walks the whole O(L) diagonal before the dedup check throws the result away, so the total work is O(L^2). `_trivial` does not stop this for real-valued data. Only constant-step runs, fewer than 4 distinct values, or small integers are skipped. I ran `_duplicate_blocks` with the project venv on two identical columns of random 4-decimal floats: L=1000 took 0.15 s, 2000 took 0.68 s and 4000 took 2.27 s, which is clearly quadratic. The input sizes are realistic. tables.py:90-101 and :129 cap xlsx/xls sheets at 20000 rows and 400 columns, and CSV input is capped at 200000 rows (tables.py:142), which is worse. Extrapolating, one 20000-row identical pair takes about 55-60 s, and k copies of a column give k(k-1)/2 such pairs. The reported failure (minutes of data-check time for a repeated annotation column) is therefore real and reachable. The memory point holds in scale but matters less: the index stores tuples for every window.
verdict.corrected_fix: Skip occurrences that fall inside a block already reported, before extending. Keep `covered: dict[tuple[int,int,int], list[tuple[int,int]]]` keyed by (ca, cb, sa - sb), holding the (s0a, s0a+ln) intervals found so far. At the top of the inner loop, after the same-column overlap check, `continue` if sa lies in any interval for that key. After extending, append (s0a, s0a+ln) to the key's list. Each diagonal is then walked once, so identical columns cost O(L) in total. The extension result is exactly the same as now. Do not use the reviewer's first suggestion on its own: skipping an occurrence because a.raw[sa-1] == b.raw[sb-1] can miss a whole block when its first window was left out of the index as trivial or because of an empty cell. Optionally, also cap the occurrences per key (for example `occ[:20]`), so that one value pattern repeated in many columns cannot blow up the x,y pair loop at lines 138-139.

findings.title: repeated_values assumes the resolution is 10^-decimals, so data on a coarser grid is flagged as copied (integrity)
findings.detail: res = 10**-dec comes from the most common decimal count. Values recorded on a 0.5 grid (12.5, 13 → '13'), the 0.2 grid of means of n=5 integer scores, or quarter steps all have one decimal, so `expected` comes out 2-5× too low. Reproduced: 200 Gaussian values rounded to 0.5 gave expected 28.6 pairs against 305 observed, and means of 5 integer scores gave 258.6 against 632. Both produced a medium `data.repeated_values` integrity finding. _norm's '.10g' also strips trailing zeros ('1.50' → '1.5'), which shifts `dec` further.
findings.failure_scenario: A behavioural-score table of per-animal means (n=5 trials), or tumour sizes measured to the nearest 0.5 mm, is reported as 'Precise values repeat more than chance allows', and this adds to the risk score.
findings.fix: Estimate the real granularity from the data: g = the GCD (with tolerance) of the nonzero differences between sorted unique values, or the smallest frequent gap, and set res = max(10**-dec, g). Also skip columns where the values sit on a lattice coarser than the printed precision.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed from code and by running it. In engine/paperinspector/datacheck.py:276-277, `_repeats` sets `res = 10**-dec`, where `dec` is the most common number of decimal places. Nothing tests whether the values actually sit on a coarser lattice. The only guard is `sigma <= 5*res` at line 280, and it is measured against the same wrong `res`, so it does not catch this case. `check()` (lines 112-114) runs `_repeats` on every numeric column without other gating, and models.py:134 lists `data.repeated_values` as a scored integrity type.

I called `_repeats` on synthetic Col objects using the project venv (.venv/bin/python):
- 200 values from N(120, 15) rounded to 0.5: 182-205 observed pairs against 33-41 expected, flagged on all 3 seeds.
- 200 means of 5 integer scores (0.2 grid): 369-379 observed against 133-163 expected, flagged on all 3 seeds.
- Control, the same data on a real 0.1 grid: never flagged.

The real resolution is 5x (0.5 grid) or 2x (0.2 grid) coarser than assumed, so `expected` comes out too low by about that factor. Per-animal means and measurements to the nearest 0.5 unit are common in supplementary tables, so this is reachable with realistic input. It produces a medium-severity, scored integrity finding: "Precise values repeat more than chance allows".

The `_norm` '.10g' point holds but is minor. It drops trailing zeros ('1.50' -> '1.5'), which can lower the most common `dec` and so inflate `res`. That pushes toward fewer flags, not more.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `_repeats`, after computing `dec` and `vals`, estimate the real lattice instead of assuming 10**-dec. Example:

    base = 10.0 ** -dec
    ints = np.round(vals / base).astype(np.int64)          # values in units of the printed precision
    u = np.unique(ints)
    g = int(np.gcd.reduce(np.diff(u))) if len(u) > 1 else 1  # exact on the integer grid, no tolerance needed
    if g <= 1:  # fallback: test a few common coarse steps that most values sit on
        for k in (5, 4, 2):
            if np.mean(ints % k == 0) > 0.9 or np.mean((ints - ints.min()) % k == 0) > 0.9:
                g = k; break
    res = base * max(g, 1)

Keep the existing `sigma <= 5*res` early return, now using the corrected `res`. Two further changes:
- Because '.10g' strips trailing zeros, compute `dec` as the maximum decimal count among values that make up at least about 10% of the column, not the mode. Better still, read the cell's display format if `Table` keeps it.
- Optionally skip the column, or demote the finding to a quality note, when `g > 1`, since a lattice coarser than the printed precision means the values are rounded or averaged.

Add regression tests: 200 Gaussian values rounded to 0.5, and 200 means of 5 integer scores, must produce no `data.repeated_values`. A column containing many pasted duplicates on a 0.1 grid must still be flagged.

findings.title: 'p < .05' is treated as non-significant, so gross decision errors are missed
findings.detail: `rep_sig = rep < 0.05 if opn in ('<', '=')`. For 'p < .05', rep is 0.05 and 0.05 < 0.05 is False, so a non-significant statistic reported as 'p < .05' gets decision=False. Reproduced: 't(20) = 1.50, p < .05' (computed p 0.149) returns decision False. The finding is then medium rather than high and the text does not say the conclusion changes. statcheck treats '<' as `rep <= alpha`.
findings.failure_scenario: 't(20) = 1.50, p < .05' should have p = 0.15. That is a changed conclusion, but it is reported as a minor inconsistency with confidence 0.7 instead of 0.85.
findings.fix: rep_sig = (rep <= 0.05) if opn == '<' else (rep < 0.05) if opn == '=' else False. Optionally treat 'p = .05' as significant, as statcheck does.

verdict.reason:
This is a real bug, and I reproduced it with the project's .venv. In engine/paperinspector/stats.py:106, `rep_sig = rep < 0.05 if opn in ("<", "=")` is False for "p < .05", because 0.05 < 0.05 is False. "p < .05" means the authors are claiming significance, so the code misreads the most common way a significant result is written.

What `recompute()` returns:
- "t(20) = 1.50, p < .05": computed p = 0.149, decision = False (wrong).
- "t(20) = 1.50, p < 0.05" and "t(20) = 1.50, p ≤ .05": same wrong result. `≤` is mapped to `<` on line 105.
- "t(20) = 1.50, p < .01": decision = True, which is correct.

The pair is still caught as inconsistent, because `_consistent` returns pmin < rep, which is False. But `check()` (lines 201-210) only counts a pair as a decision error when `decision` is True. So the finding drops from "high" with confidence 0.85 to "medium" with confidence 0.7, and the text leaves out "change the conclusion at p = 0.05". That is exactly the failure the reviewer described.

The input is realistic. "p < .05" is probably the most common way a significant result is reported, so this misses the largest group of real decision errors.
verdict.corrected_fix: In stats.py:106, replace the line with `rep_sig = (rep <= 0.05) if opn == "<" else (rep < 0.05) if opn == "=" else False`. An operator of '<' (which also covers ≤, since line 105 maps it to '<') then counts a reported threshold of exactly .05 as a significance claim, while '=' keeps the strict comparison. As an option, follow statcheck and also treat "p = .05" as significant with `rep <= 0.05`. Add tests: "t(20) = 1.50, p < .05" should give decision True, and "t(20) = 1.50, p > .05" should give decision False.

findings.title: GRIM uses Python's banker's rounding, so correctly rounded means are called impossible
findings.detail: `round(k / n, d)` uses round-half-even on binary floats. 1/8 = 0.125 gives 0.12, but authors and statistics packages report 0.13. Reproduced: grim('the mean number of lesions was 0.13 (n = 8)') and grim('mean score 2.13 (n = 8)') both return a GRIM hit, which is an integrity finding. GRIM_CTX (line 113) also accepts 'scale', 'likert', 'score' and 'per mouse', where multi-item averages or per-subject means are not integer-granular. That is a second source of false positives.
findings.failure_scenario: A paper with n = 8 animals reports a mean count of 2.13 (17/8 = 2.125). The scan reports 'Means that are impossible for the sample size (GRIM)', medium integrity, confidence 0.65.
findings.fix: Accept a mean if it lies within half a unit of the last reported digit of any k/n, by testing abs(k/n - mean) <= 0.5*10**-d + 1e-9 for k in floor/ceil. Or use decimal.Decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP and ROUND_HALF_EVEN. Drop 'scale', 'likert' and 'score' from GRIM_CTX unless n refers to single-item integer responses.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real, and I reproduced it with the project venv. In engine/paperinspector/stats.py:129, `possible = any(abs(round(k / n, d) - mean) < 1e-9 ...)` uses Python's built-in round(). That is round-half-even, and it works on binary floats. 1/8 = 0.125 and 17/8 = 2.125 are exact in binary, so round() gives 0.12 and 2.12. A paper that rounds half-up the usual way reports 0.13 or 2.13, and the code calls that impossible.

Calls I ran:
- grim('the mean number of lesions was 0.13 (n = 8)') returns a hit.
- grim('mean score 2.13 (n = 8)') returns a hit.
- 2.12 (n = 8) returns nothing, so the code accepts only the half-even rounding.

Both hit sentences pass the context filter: "lesions" and "score" match GRIM_CTX (line 113). stats.py:212-219 then emits Finding "stats.grim", severity "medium", confidence 0.65, titled "Means that are impossible for the sample size (GRIM)". The description is also wrong for these cases: it says "closest possible: 2.12" (line 218), using the same half-even rounding. Any n divisible by 8 or 16 can produce an exact .xx5 tie, and n = 8 is a common animal-study size.

The second claim is weaker but valid. GRIM_CTX includes 'score', 'scale', 'likert', 'items?' and 'per mouse'. Multi-item scale averages and per-subject means of repeated counts are not means of n integers, so GRIM does not apply to them. That is another source of false positives, though it is a judgment about scope rather than a coding bug.
verdict.corrected_fix: In grim() (stats.py:129), replace the round()-equality test with a tolerance test that accepts both rounding conventions. Set tol = 0.5 * 10 ** -d + 1e-9, then set possible = any(abs(k / n - mean) <= tol for k in (math.floor(mean * n), math.ceil(mean * n))). This matches the tolerance that percent() at line 146 already uses. Make the same change in the 'closest possible' text at line 218: format round(mean * n) / n with enough digits, or with Decimal ROUND_HALF_UP, so the message does not show the half-even value. Optionally, apply GRIM only when the context names a count or a single integer item: drop 'scale', 'likert' and 'items?' from GRIM_CTX, or require 'score' or 'rating' to sit next to 'single-item' or 'item'. The scale change is a precision trade-off, not part of the core bug fix.

findings.title: US-style dates are parsed day-first, creating fake 'accepted in 1 day' integrity signals
findings.detail: DATE_RE accepts `\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{4}` and _parse_date tries only '%d/%m/%Y'. 'Received 5/1/2021; Accepted 6/1/2021' (May 1 to June 1, US style) is parsed as 5 Jan to 6 Jan. Reproduced: timeline() returns `record.fast_acceptance` 'Accepted 1 day(s) after submission', severity medium. record.fast_acceptance is in INTEGRITY (models.py 137), so it adds to the score. The reverse ordering can also yield 'Accepted before it was received'.
findings.failure_scenario: A US journal prints numeric received/accepted dates. The report says peer review took 1 day and links it to paper mills.
findings.fix: For slash dates, try both '%m/%d/%Y' and '%d/%m/%Y'. If both parse and give different intervals, either drop the timeline finding or pick the interpretation that is consistent (non-negative and plausible). Prefer Crossref assertion dates over text when both exist.

verdict.reason: I confirmed this by reading the code and by running it. engine/paperinspector/reporting.py:137 has DATE_RE accept `\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{4}`, and _parse_date at line 143 tries only '%d/%m/%Y' for slash dates. timeline() is called from pipeline.py:387. Dates found in the text are stored first (lines 154-160), and Crossref meta dates fill in only the keys still missing (line 163), so a misread text date wins over a correct Crossref date. I ran timeline() on 'Received 5/1/2021; Accepted 6/1/2021' (May 1 to June 1). It returned received=2021-01-05, accepted=2021-01-06, days_to_accept=1, and a record.fast_acceptance finding at severity 'medium'. record.fast_acceptance is in INTEGRITY (models.py:137), so the score goes up. A second problem shows up with an unambiguous US date: 'Received 12/20/2021; Accepted 1/5/2022' leaves received unparsed (month 20 fails) and silently misreads accepted as 2022-05-01. Received can then come from Crossref, so the interval mixes sources and the 'Accepted before it was received' or fast-acceptance logic runs on wrong data. This is reachable, but only for the minority of journals that print numeric slash dates. Most print month names.
verdict.corrected_fix: In reporting.py, make _parse_date return every valid reading of a slash date. Try '%m/%d/%Y' and '%d/%m/%Y', and for a component above 12 only one will parse. In timeline(), when a received/accepted pair came from slash dates and both readings exist, (a) prefer the Crossref meta dates (meta['dates']) if present, and (b) otherwise pick the convention (US or day-first) applied to both dates together that gives a non-negative interval. If both conventions are non-negative but give different intervals, emit no fast_acceptance or negative-interval finding (record only info['date_format_ambiguous']=True). Also, when a text date fails to parse, do not mix it with a meta date from the other key unless both come from the same source.

findings.title: European decimal commas become thousands; UTF-16 and BOM CSVs are read as garbage and marked 'analysed'
findings.detail: NUM_RE treats `\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})+` as a thousands separator, so '0,125' becomes 125.0 and '1,234' becomes 1234, while '12,5' is dropped (None). That is a mix of corrupted and missing values in the same column. Reproduced with a ';'-delimited CSV: the 'p value' column became [807, 581, 387, …]. read_delimited (line 135) decodes only as UTF-8 with errors='replace'. An Excel 'Unicode Text' export (UTF-16LE with BOM, a common .txt supplement) becomes '\x00G\x000…', every number is lost, and sources still marks the file 'analysed'. A UTF-8 BOM makes number('﻿1.2') None, which drops the first value of a headerless file. Accounting-style '(12)' parses as +12.
findings.failure_scenario: A Source Data CSV from a German or French Excel: values with 3 decimals become ×1000 integers that feed the duplicate, derived, impossible and repeats detectors, and values with 1-2 decimals disappear. A UTF-16 .txt supplement yields no data and no warning.
findings.fix: In read_delimited, detect BOMs (codecs.BOM_UTF16_LE/BE → 'utf-16', BOM_UTF8 → 'utf-8-sig'). If UTF-8 fails, fall back to cp1252. When the sniffed delimiter is ';' or the column shows a decimal-comma pattern (`^-?\d+,\d+$` in most numeric-looking cells), parse ',' as the decimal point for that table. Pass a decimal-separator hint into number(). Report undecodable files as 'not analysed'.

verdict.reason: I ran the code and every part of the report reproduced. Running from engine/, number() in engine/paperinspector/tables.py (NUM_RE at line 16, parse at lines 39-50) gives these results. '0,125' -> 125.0, '0,807' -> 807.0 and '1,234' -> 1234.0, because the first alternative \d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})+ matches and then every comma is removed. '12,5' -> None. '﻿1.2' -> None, since a BOM is not in [\s(] (a BOM is not whitespace in Python's re). '(12)' -> 12.0, because the parentheses are dropped and no sign is applied. So a column of decimal-comma values ends up as a mix of x1000 integers (3 decimals) and missing values (1-2 decimals). read_delimited (lines 134-142) decodes only with utf-8 errors='replace'. A UTF-16 .txt file (with BOM) became cells like '\x00g\x00e\x00n\x00e\x00' and '\x001\x00.\x005\x00', so no number in it parses. read_any (line 221) sends .csv/.tsv/.txt to read_delimited. sources.py line 161 sets status 'analysed' whenever any Table is returned. A UTF-16 file still produces rows of garbage, so it gets 'analysed' with nothing flagged. All of this is reachable with realistic input: Source Data files exported from German or French Excel, and Excel 'Unicode Text' .txt supplements.
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. In read_delimited: check for a BOM first. BOM_UTF16_LE/BE -> decode as 'utf-16'. BOM_UTF8 -> decode as 'utf-8-sig'. Otherwise try strict utf-8, then fall back to cp1252. Also strip '﻿' inside number().
2. Find the decimal separator per table. If the delimiter is ';' or most numeric-looking cells match ^[-−–]?\d+,\d+$, treat ',' as the decimal mark: remove '.' and spaces used as thousands separators, then turn ',' into '.'. Store the result as Table.meta['decimal'] = ','. Have number() take a decimal argument, and pass it from callers that read table cells (for example via a Table.number helper).
3. Read '(x)' as -x only when the parentheses close around a plain number.
4. In sources.py around line 161, report 'not analysed: could not decode text' when decoding failed or when a large share of cells contain '\x00' or '�'.

findings.title: repeated_spread flags tolerances and specifications as fabricated SDs (integrity)
findings.detail: Every 'x ± y' in the text is collected, with no check that y is an SD or SEM of measured groups. Repeated tolerances such as 'pH 7.40 ± 0.05' for several buffers, '37 ± 0.5 °C', or doses 'mean ± 10' trigger it. Reproduced: four buffer pH specs give {'spread': '0.05', 'count': 4}. stats.repeated_se is in INTEGRITY, with medium severity and confidence 0.6.
findings.failure_scenario: A Methods section lists buffer recipes with '± 0.05' tolerances. The report shows 'The same spread repeated after different means' as an integrity signal.
findings.fix: Require statistical context near the matches (SD|SEM|s.e.m.|mean in the same sentence or table caption). Exclude units such as °C, pH, mM, %, and spreads where y is a round tolerance (0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10). Require the values to come from a table-like run rather than prose.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code and by running it. In engine/paperinspector/stats.py:155, PM_RE matches every "x ± y" (also +/- and +-) anywhere in the whitespace-collapsed full text. repeated_spread (stats.py:158-173) looks for a spread that appears 4 or more times after 4 or more distinct means within any window of 12 consecutive pairs. The only filter is on the spread's format: 2 or more decimals, or a value of 10 or more. Nothing checks the surrounding text: no SD/SEM/mean wording, no table context, no units, no "pH" before the number.

I ran it in the project venv:
- 'HEPES pH 7.40 ± 0.05, Tris pH 8.00 ± 0.05, MES pH 6.20 ± 0.05, acetate pH 5.00 ± 0.05' returned {'spread': '0.05', 'count': 4, means 5.00/6.20/7.40/8.00}.
- 'Doses were 100 ± 10, 200 ± 10, 300 ± 10, 400 ± 10 mg' returned spread '10', count 4.
- Four nominal sizes '± 0.25 nm' also flagged.

One part of the report is wrong: '37 ± 0.5 °C' on its own is filtered out, because 0.5 has only 1 decimal. The "± 10" and 2-decimal tolerance cases are real.

Effect on the report: check() at stats.py:230-236 emits "stats.repeated_se" with severity medium and confidence 0.6. That check is in INTEGRITY (models.py:135), so risk_score (models.py:149-156) counts it toward the integrity score. The finding says "Independent groups almost never share an SD/SE to the last digit", so a Methods list of specification tolerances becomes a scored manipulation signal. This is reachable with realistic text: buffer recipes, gradient or dose schedules, and instrument tolerances.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Do not apply the blanket exclusions in the proposed fix. Excluding round spreads (0.05, 0.1, 10) or all prose would also suppress real repeated-SD fabrication. A narrower fix in repeated_spread (stats.py:158):

1. Drop a pair when the text just before the mean names a specification rather than a measurement. Use a regex such as r'\b(pH|at|to|set to|adjusted to|tolerance|±\s*$)\s*$' on text[max(0,m.start()-12):m.start()]. Also drop it when the text after y is a tolerance or physical unit typical of settings: °C, ppm, Da, rpm, x g, mM, nm.
2. Require a statistical cue near the run: r'\b(mean|SD|S\.?D\.?|SEM|s\.e\.m\.|standard (deviation|error)|±\s*SE)\b'. Look in the sentence or caption around the window's first match, or in one global declaration such as 'mean ± SD' or 'data are presented as mean ± SEM'.
3. Skip runs whose means form an exact arithmetic progression of round numbers (for example 100/200/300/400, or 58/60/62/64). Those are nominal settings, not measured group means.

Also add regression tests for the pH-buffer and dose-schedule strings, plus a positive control: a table of means each followed by an identical '± 0.37' under a 'mean ± SD' caption.

findings.title: generator_digits cannot fire, and _norm silently truncates values to 10 significant digits
findings.detail: Col.raw comes from _norm(), which uses format(v, '.10g') (line 64), so no raw string has more than 10 significant digits. `_sig_digits(r) >= 13` in _generator is therefore never true. Reproduced: a column of repr(random()*100) values like '79.06413797592705' normalises to '79.06413798' and no finding is raised. The same truncation merges distinct long IDs: 40 distinct 13-digit ms timestamps collapse to 2 distinct normalised strings. Duplicate and repeat logic on long IDs or high-precision values is therefore wrong.
findings.failure_scenario: Data pasted from RAND() output (the case the docstring describes) is never flagged. Two different high-precision columns that differ only past the 10th digit compare as identical runs.
findings.fix: Keep the original cell text (stripped) for precision checks (_generator, _digits, _repeats' decimal count), and normalise with repr(float) or '.15g' for equality. Run _generator on the raw cell strings rather than c.raw.

verdict.reason: Confirmed from the code. In engine/paperinspector/datacheck.py, columns() (line 81) fills Col.raw only with _norm(c). _norm (lines 59-64) returns format(number(s), '.10g'), which has at most 10 significant digits; with exponent notation _sig_digits splits on 'e', so it still counts at most 10. _generator (lines 432-449) uses columns() and checks `_sig_digits(r) >= 13` on c.raw (line 442), so `long` is always empty and data.generator_digits can never be emitted, whatever the input. Verified: format(79.06413797592705,'.10g') gives '79.06413798', which is 10 digits. No test in tests/ or tools/ covers generator_digits, so nothing catches this. The precision loss is also real: 40 distinct 13-digit ms timestamps (1700000000000+37i) normalise to only 2 distinct strings. Equality-based checks (_duplicate_blocks line 129, _duplicate_columns, the distinct counts at lines 189/347, _repeats) therefore treat values that differ past the 10th significant digit as equal. Two things soften that secondary effect. _trivial (len(set(win)) < 4) and the `len(set(c.raw)) >= 5` guard suppress many collapsed windows. And most real measured data has fewer than 10 significant digits. The primary claim, a dead detector, holds without qualification.
verdict.corrected_fix: Keep the stripped original cell text in Col (for example a new field `text: list[str]`, set from str(c).strip(), or repr(float) for numeric cells read from xlsx) next to the normalised key. In _generator, count significant digits on that original text, or on repr(v) for float cells, instead of c.raw. Change _norm to format(v, '.15g') (or repr(v)) so equality keys keep full double precision while float noise such as 0.1+0.2 still collapses. Note that a float cell from openpyxl has no 'as typed' text, so repr(v) is the right source there. Add a regression test: a .csv table with 25 values of repr(random()*100) should yield data.generator_digits.

findings.title: split() keeps the last numbered list, not the longest run; cited() makes superscript-style papers look padded
findings.detail: The comment says 'keep the longest run', but the loop resets `run` whenever an entry numbered 1 appears. A numbered list after the references (figure legends, supplementary notes, Methods steps) replaces the real bibliography. Reproduced: 40 references followed by a 6-item legend list gives split() 6 entries. Separately, cited() only understands bracketed numbers. In Nature, Cell or PNAS style papers (superscript citations), any 3 bracketed numbers in the body ('[1]', '[Ca2+]i [2]', interval '[0, 3]') pass the `len(c) >= 3` gate. Reproduced: 'refs.uncited' (medium) '37 of 40 references are not cited'.
findings.failure_scenario: A Nature-format paper is reported as 'Many references are never cited … Padding a bibliography inflates citation counts', which accuses the authors of citation padding when they used superscripts.
findings.fix: Track all runs and keep the longest (max by len). Gate the uncited and missing checks on bracket citations being the dominant style: require len(c) >= 0.3*n, or at least 10 distinct bracket citations that cover a contiguous range starting at 1.

verdict.reason:
Both halves of the report hold up when run against the code.

1. split(), engine/paperinspector/refs.py:33-39. The loop sets `run = [e]` whenever an entry is numbered 1, so the run that survives is the last list that starts at 1, not the longest one. The comment on line 32 says it keeps the longest run; the code does not. The tail is everything after the last References heading, so a numbered list there replaces the bibliography: figure legends, Supplementary Methods steps, anything shaped like "1. ...". I checked this with Paper(source='x', pages=[...]): 40 references followed by a 6-item "Supplementary Methods" list gives split() 6 entries. check() then compares the paper against that 6-item list. split() is also used in history.py:47 and in retractions(), so they get the wrong list too.

2. cited(), refs.py:42-52, with the gate at refs.py:66. Only bracketed numbers count as citations. Superscript citations come out of PDF text as plain digits ("previously12,13"), and CITE_RE does not match them. Any 3 bracketed numbers anywhere in the body pass `len(c) >= 3`: an interval like "[0, 1]", an equation number "[2]", a step reference "[5]". The body is everything before the last References heading, so it includes Methods. I checked this too: a 40-reference Nature-style paper whose body contains "[0, 1] ... [2] ... [5]" gets a refs.uncited finding at medium severity: "37 of 40 references are not cited in the text (highest citation in the text: [5]). Padding a bibliography inflates citation counts..." pipeline.py:373 calls this check for every paper. The result is a false accusation of citation padding, with medium severity once at least half the references are uncited.

The report's examples "[Ca2+]i" and "[3H]" do not match CITE_RE, but interval and equation brackets are enough to trigger it, so the bug is real as described.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In split(), collect every run and keep the longest. On an entry numbered 1, close the current run and start a new one. Then return `max(runs, key=len)`.

In check(), only run the uncited and missing checks when bracket citations look like the paper's real citation style. For example, require all of these:
- `len(c) >= max(10, 0.3 * n)`
- `1 in c`
- c is mostly contiguous from 1, e.g. `len(c & set(range(1, max(c) + 1))) >= 0.6 * max(c)`

Ignore 0 when collecting citation numbers, and drop parts larger than n + 20. When there are some bracket numbers but not enough to pass this gate, emit nothing, or at most an info-level note. Do not emit refs.uncited.

findings.title: ETHICS pattern matches 'license', so the missing-ethics check is effectively off for open-access papers
findings.detail: ETHICS contains `licen[cs]e` and `approved by`. Almost every OA article includes 'licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License', so report.no_ethics never fires for them. Reproduced: an animal-work text with a CC license footer gives no finding, and the same text without the footer gives report.no_ethics. Conversely, HUMAN matches 'patients' in any introduction, so computational or review papers without ethics statements get a medium 'No ethics approval mentioned'.
findings.failure_scenario: An OA mouse study with no IACUC statement passes silently. A modelling paper that cites 'patients' in its introduction is asked for ethics approval.
findings.fix: Replace `licen[cs]e` with `(?:project|animal|home office)\s+licen[cs]e` and make 'approved by' require (ethic|committee|board|IACUC) within ~60 chars. Require ANIMAL or HUMAN matches inside a Methods section, or at least 3 occurrences, before flagging.

verdict.reason: The bug is real. In engine/paperinspector/reporting.py, lines 194-195 define ETHICS with a bare `licen[cs]e` alternative. statements() (lines 218-223) only adds report.no_ethics when `re.search(ETHICS, text, re.I)` finds nothing anywhere in the full paper text. Open-access PDFs almost always carry a footer like "This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License". I ran the real ETHICS regex on such a string and it matched 'license', so the ethics check is silenced for those papers. The bare `approved by` alternative is just as loose (e.g. "approved by the FDA", "approved by all authors"). The reverse case also holds: the HUMAN regex matched 'patients' in an introduction-only sentence, so a computational or review paper can get the medium-severity finding. That part is a lower-confidence false positive, not a crash, but it is reachable. The only existing test (tests/test_data.py:59) checks the positive case and does not cover a license footer.
verdict.corrected_fix: In reporting.py:194-195, replace `licen[cs]e` with `(?:project|animal|personal|establishment|home office)\s+licen[cs]e`. Replace bare `approved by` with `approved by (?:the |an? )?[^.]{0,60}?(?:ethic|committee|board|IACUC|IRB)`. Optionally drop the CC-licence footer before matching, e.g. `re.sub(r"(?:licensed under|Creative Commons)[^.]{0,200}\.", " ", text, flags=re.I)`. To reduce false positives from HUMAN/ANIMAL, require at least 2 matches, or a match near method words (enrolled|recruited|treated|injected|housed|sacrificed|obtained from), before flagging. Add a regression test: an animal-methods text with a CC licence footer must still produce report.no_ethics.

findings.title: 'Impossible' percentages and negatives flagged on honest relative measures and blank-subtracted data
findings.detail: PCT_H matches any header with '%'. '% viability', '% of control', '% recovery' and '% growth' legitimately exceed 100, and '% inhibition' can be negative. NONNEG_H includes 'concentration', but blank-subtracted ELISA concentrations are routinely slightly negative. Reproduced: a '% viability' column with values 104.2 and 107.9 gives 'Impossible values: percentages outside 0-100'.
findings.failure_scenario: A cell-viability Source Data sheet normalised to control is reported as having impossible values.
findings.fix: Exempt headers matching (of control|relative|viability|recovery|growth|inhibition|change|increase|decrease|normali[sz]ed). Only enforce > 100 for headers like '% of total', 'proportion' or 'frequency'. For concentration, ignore small negatives (for example > -5% of the column range).

findings.title: figure_count counts Supplementary and Extended Data figure numbers; n_supp_figures is unused
findings.detail: The regex `\bFig(?:ure)?s?\.?\s*(\d{1,2})` matches the 'Figure 9' inside 'Supplementary Figure 9' and 'Extended Data Fig. 9'. The n_supp_figures parameter is never read, and pipeline.py 390 passes 0. Reproduced: 'See Figure 2 and Supplementary Figure 9' with 4 figures gives 'Text cites Figure 9, but 4 figures were found'. The `(?![\d.])` lookahead also drops sentence-final citations such as 'Fig. 10.'.
findings.failure_scenario: Almost every paper with supplementary figures numbered above the main-figure count gets this note.
findings.fix: Add a negative lookbehind for (Supplementary|Suppl\.?|Extended Data|Fig\.\s*S) before the match, or remove those spans first. Change the lookahead to `(?!\d|\.\d)`.

findings.title: record() misses the 'withdrawal' and 'partial_retraction' notice types
findings.detail: Only 'retraction', 'removal' and 'expression_of_concern' are recognised. Crossref update-to types also include 'withdrawal' and 'partial_retraction' (and 'clarification'). A withdrawn or partially retracted paper produces no record finding, and line 119 uses a different normalisation (`lower()` only) from line 117 (`replace('-', '_')`).
findings.failure_scenario: An Elsevier article that was withdrawn shows no publication-record warning.
findings.fix: Normalise once, t = type.lower().replace('-', '_'), and treat {'retraction', 'removal', 'withdrawal', 'partial_retraction'} as retracted (partial maybe 'high'). Add 'clarification' to corrections.

findings.title: Repeat discount is keyed on (check, severity), so per-column false positives add up without limit; the verdict is stale after AI triage
findings.detail: The docstring says repeats of one check count less and less, but the key includes severity. The discount 1/(1+0.6n) also grows roughly logarithmically, so 20 medium data.repeated_values hits (one per column, typical for the lattice false positive above) add about 4.8× one hit, about 24 points, pushing the score to about 41 ('Worth a closer look'). Separately, agent.py 309-311 recomputes score_ai without AI false positives but leaves report['verdict'] from the unfiltered findings, so the UI can show 'Serious concerns' next to a low AI score.
findings.failure_scenario: A large Source Data workbook with honest lattice data in many columns reaches a mid-range risk score from one detector. After the AI marks the only critical finding false_positive, the verdict text still reads 'Serious concerns'.
findings.fix: Key the discount on check only, and cap each check's total contribution (for example to its strongest finding × 1.5). In agent.py also set report['verdict_ai'] = verdict(score_ai, …) from dict-aware logic (verdict() currently needs Finding objects).

findings.title: Merged cells are mishandled in DOCX (duplicated) and JATS (rowspan ignored), which misaligns columns
findings.detail: python-docx `row.cells` returns the same _tc for every grid column a merged cell spans, so its value is copied into neighbouring columns, which can produce identical runs across columns. read_jats_tables (lines 178-185) pads colspan but ignores rowspan, so every row under a row-spanning cell shifts left by one column and values from different variables are mixed into one Col. `int(c.get('colspan'))` also raises on non-integer values ('2.0'), and that call (sources.py 121) has no try/except.
findings.failure_scenario: A JATS Table 1 with a row-spanning 'Group' cell puts SD values into the mean column for later rows, which produces spurious impossible, spread or derived findings. A Word table with horizontally merged numeric cells over 6+ rows triggers duplicate_block.
findings.fix: In DOCX, deduplicate cells by `id(c._tc)` within a row (emit '' for repeats). In JATS, keep a pending-rowspan map {col: remaining} and insert '' placeholders. Parse spans with `int(float(x))` inside try/except.

findings.title: Hidden-text and AI-boilerplate checks fire on ordinary layouts and published peer-review files
findings.detail: hidden_text treats any span with min(r,g,b) ≥ 245 as hidden. White labels on dark figure panels (scale bars '50 µm', panel letters on micrographs) and white text in coloured journal banners are visible, so 6+ words of them produce a medium 'Hidden text in the PDF'. Separately, AI_PHRASES includes 'in this (?:revised|rewritten) version', which is standard in author responses. pipeline.py 366 runs textcheck on every supplementary PDF, including Nature's 'Peer Review File', so ≥ 2 hits give a HIGH text.ai_boilerplate.
findings.failure_scenario: A microscopy paper with white panel labels gets 'Hidden text in the PDF'. A Nature paper whose supplements include the peer review file gets 'Chatbot boilerplate left in the text', high.
findings.fix: Check the background under the span: render the span bbox at low DPI and require low contrast, or skip spans that overlap an image block. Drop the 'revised version' phrase, or skip supplementary files whose name or text matches 'peer review|response to reviewers|rebuttal'.

findings.title: Recompute always assumes two-tailed tests
findings.detail: _p() doubles the t, z and r tails unconditionally. A correctly reported one-tailed test ('one-tailed t(15) = 1.90, p = .038') is flagged as inconsistent, and because 0.077 vs 0.038 crosses 0.05 it is labelled a decision error (HIGH). statcheck accepts p/2 when 'one-tailed', 'one-sided' or 'directional' appears nearby.
findings.failure_scenario: A pre-registered one-sided hypothesis test gets a HIGH 'Reported p-values do not match their test statistics' integrity finding.
findings.fix: In recompute, if the ±150 chars around the match contain one-?(tailed|sided)|directional, also accept comp/2. In general mark the result consistent if either the one- or two-tailed value fits, and record which one did.

findings.title: Hidden rows and columns are reported even when they are empty
findings.detail: The elif branch reports any hidden row or column dimension without checking that it holds data. Many authors hide the unused columns to the right of a table (Excel writes one <col min=… max=16384 hidden=1> entry), which gives 'Hidden rows or columns … Excluded data points are sometimes hidden'.
findings.failure_scenario: A tidy Source Data sheet with the unused columns hidden is reported as possibly hiding excluded data.
findings.fix: Keep only hidden rows or columns that intersect non-empty cells in `rows` (convert column letters with openpyxl.utils.column_index_from_string and check the cells within the data range). Report counts of data-bearing hidden cells.
